content_html_sanitized:
Originally Posted January 23, 2003, edited and updated by yours truly.

 

From the beginning, I have said that MarijuanaNews is by me, but not about me. Nonetheless, it is obviously a very personal effort, and this Monday was a perfect illustration of why I do what I do.

 

The day began badly when NORML's Allen St. Pierre told me that my friend Todd McCormick had been moved to a different federal prison. (The moves are pointlessly prolonged and are called diesel therapy by the prisoners.) Moreover, he is being held in solitary confinement in the hole for 30 days for a procedural violation.

His new prison address is
Todd McCormick
Prisoner #
P.O. Box
California, 92301
FCI Victorville

Please write him a note of encouragement and let him know that he is not forgotten.

 

Happy to say that this is no longer relevant, but never forget!

 

I told Allen that I wished that this issue was just an abstraction, not about my friends. The unreality of that wish was brought home to me up close and personal just a little later.

 

I met with Steve Tuck that afternoon to accompany him to the Compassion Society, where he was going to get some medicine. They had a fire there last week and I wanted to check out the damage. (I am not a member, but I have many friends on the staff.)

 

Shortly after we turned onto Hastings Street (legal turn), a police car pulled alongside Steve's little truck (which has California plates) then dropped back and turned on its lights and signalled us to pull over. I know that Steve was not driving very fast, and I am not aware of his having broken any laws, but it must be easy to make an improper lane change since so many marijuana arrests are derived from such events.

 

(I have seldom seen a traffic stop in Vancouver, although I did recently see two uniformed cops go into a porn theatre on Granville Street. I suppose they were investigating the problem of one-handed clapping.

 

(Hastings is a major street in Downtown Vancouver and one block was (in)famous as the Pot Block and home of Marc Emery’s seed company and Pot Tv, etc.)

 

The traffic and street parking on Hastings made it difficult for Steve to find a place to pull over, so we went about a block further until we could turn right onto Hamilton, which dead-ends into the Pot-TV studios.

 

The Vancouver cop came up to the driver-side window and immediately announced that he had smelled marijuana smoke, even though we had not been smoking and there was no such smell noticeable to me.

 

Steve had been badly abused when he was in custody here last April, so he was understandably very polite and cautious with the officer, but he ordered Steve out of the truck, as Steve tried to explain his situation to him.

 

Someone at the Marijuana Party offices must have seen what was happening, because my friend Chris Bennett appeared almost immediately, video camera in hand. He arrived just in time to hear the cop being very verbally abusive toward Steve with a stream of obscenities.

 

Chris asked, Can you repeat that for the camera?

 

The officer declined and his language improved greatly, although his attitude did not.

 

Meanwhile, Steve explained about his legal refugee status, and showed him his papers and his Compassion Society membership card, but that made no difference, and his California driver's license. (The truck belongs to Steve's wife and is insured.)

 

Despite this, the cop ordered Steve to get up on the sidewalk, and proceeded to search him. Steve had a joint in his pocket, which in Vancouver is no big deal, even for non-patients. The cop acted like he had found a kilo of crack.

 

We were across the street from Blunt Bros. and the New Amsterdam, where the DEAland Drug Czar and the head of the Vancouver narcotics and vice-squad had seen Steve smoke hash a few weeks ago. So this was more than a little silly, but at this point just silly.
See
Steve Tuck Smokes Hash with John Walters As Czar Visits Vancouver's New Amsterdam Cafe. Another One We Couldn't Make Up. Of course, Walters Didn't Smoke with Steve, But.. Special to MarijuanaNews

 

Chris kept taping and asked the cops embarrassing questions about crime on the streets in that area, and the Vancouver police record of violence. Because the cops wouldn't let Chris get close, the audio was bad, but I referred listeners to PivotLegal.org which has a study of the Vancouver police violence on their web site.

 

At this point, I had gotten out of the truck and was standing on the sidewalk, when Steve told the cop that he had a pocket-knife, which he slowly pulled out of his coat pocket and handed it to the cop. Such a knife is legal in Canada, but the cop used this as an excuse to hand-cuff Steve. He explained that anything that made an officer feel threatened was a weapon!

 

After having begun the day finding out that Todd McCormick was in the hole, watching Steve Tuck being handcuffed was just too much.

 

The cop that I was talking to was very polite, but I pulled out my cell phone and called John Conroy, QC, the great BC lawyer who is handling one of the Canadian Supreme Court cases.
See
Canadian Supreme Court Punts On Cannabis Cases Until Spring. The Games Governments Play Prove The Need for International Debate on Cannabis Prohibition. Special to MarijuanaNews

 

John left a meeting to take my call, and he talked me through the situation. I let the good cop know whom I was calling. John asked to speak with him, but the cop would not talk.

Nonetheless, John made it very clear that none of the alleged offences justified handcuffing anyone, much less arresting them.

 

At his instruction, I asked if I was free to go, which I was, but I couldn't leave with Steve there, of course.

 

At this point, with Chris bobbing and weaving with the camera, and the top lawyer in BC on the phone, the cops began to have second thoughts. A supervisor cop pulled up to observe but stayed in his car. The ill-mannered cop spent several minutes on the radio to someone, as Steve stood shivering in the cold with his wrists being strangled by the cuffs.

 

John Conroy could tell that I was very upset, and kept saying, Now don't you do something that will get you arrested! I was flattered. Actually, as I explained, I wasn't going to get violent, but I joked that I might cry.

 

It was so indescribably sad to see someone like Steve, who is seriously crippled, standing there deprived of freedom again.

 

First and foremost, it is sad at the personal level, because everyone is entitled to be treated as a human being, but especially people like Todd and Steve, who are my heroes.

 

It is sad for Vancouver, that the police are hassling anyone about cannabis, much less a patient, on a street where hard drugs are sold openly and fifty women were kidnapped and murdered before the police were forced to pay attention. (The victims were mostly prostitutes and addicts, and many were natives. Three other dehumanized groups.)

 

It is sad for Canada, that it still does not have a medical cannabis program that takes care of sick people.
See
Canadian Health Minister Seeks Asylum In DEAland; Says Making Her Think About Medical Cannabis Constitutes Torture. In DC They Don't Allow That Sort of Thing. Thinking, That Is.

 

It is tragic for the Land of the Free that Steve is in exile here.

After all of this, the ill-mannered cop suddenly decided that he would let Steve go with a traffic ticket for not having a BC driver's license. Fair enough, and if that had been all that had happened, no one would complain.

 

But why was Steve handcuffed in the first place? And would it have gone differently if Chris had not had a camera and I had not had a Queen's Counsel on the phone?

 

Unfortunately, the police added injury to insult and seized a quantity of seeds that Steve was taking to give to patients at the Compassion Society, and he will have to fight to get them back. When Steve first came up here he gave a huge quantity of seeds to Health Canada, but that apparently doesn't count either.

 

Then that was over, and we went on to the Compassion Society.

 

It was there that I saw Mike. I don't know his last name, but I noticed him after he had bought his medicine. He was hunched over his walker and spoke with a slur that made me think that he had advanced MS. I moved to open the door for him, but he said that he could do it himself. Keeping dignity and self-reliance is very important to patients, and it is cannabis that makes it possible for so many of them to do that.

 

After Mike left, Steve explained to me that, like Steve, he had been in a terrible accident that left him severely crippled and with brain damage, hence his slurred speech.

 

Steve says that having cannabis has made a huge difference in Mike's quality of life and that he is always cheerful and has a kind word for everyone. Is Mike handicapped, or is everyone else?

 

And, yes, I finally did cry out of anger and frustration, but now you know why I do what I do.

 

Now, in 2025, Steve and Todd are free, and safe in the Land of the Free, and Canada has legalized both medical and recreational cannabis. But…. are any of us really free and safe until everyone is?
